source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: Debugging has four steps. Most time goes to building and updating a mental model of the system, not to fixing.
numbers: 17 tasks; 7 professional developers + 5 live-coding streamers; time split 12% reproduce, 57% mental model, 13% fix, 18% validate; 1.65 fix-validate cycles per task; 9 of 17 tasks returned to model update after a failed fix; 4 unfinished sessions ended in model update.
limits: Observational, small N, self-chosen tasks; no controls; theory validated on 5 further streams.
agent_relevance: Budget most agent steps for evidence gathering. A failed check should send the agent back to S2 (model update), not straight to a new patch.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: The model has two parts: uncertainty (what I know I do not know) and speculations (loose guesses). Developers never stated formal hypotheses.
numbers: All developers tracked uncertainty on all tasks; none articulated formal hypotheses (stated in paper).
quote: developers focus on clarifying what is known and unknown about the codebase
limits: Think-aloud data; P5 deliberately held guesses unchecked 'to not jump to conclusions'.
agent_relevance: S2 should keep a running list of unknowns and a separate list of untested guesses. Guesses guide where to look; they are not tested one by one.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: Breadth-first, good-enough model building. Developers avoid learning more than needed (knowledge avoidance).
numbers: P1: 52 min finding the commit that introduced the bug, 12 min looking for earlier fixes, 13 min reproducing at another scope. Others used expert help, AI help, temporary DOM fixes.
limits: Anecdotal examples from a few participants; contradicts older advice to understand thoroughly first.
agent_relevance: Cap exploration: stop reading once the model is enough to pick the next check. Cheap detours (version history, narrower repro) can beat deep reading.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: Two tracing modes: forward (cause to outcome) and backward (failure to cause). Mode depends on codebase familiarity.
numbers: Forward dominant for P2, P5 (>=50% familiarity); backward dominant for P3, P4 (<20% familiarity); streamers made more progress transitions than participants, median 9 vs 4, p=0.014 (Mann-Whitney U).
limits: Few participants per familiarity band; no effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Agent in an unfamiliar repo should trace backward from the failing output; switch to forward tracing once the region is known.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: Developers use LLMs as an extension of web search. They helped with small syntax and API facts, but an AI-written fix failed for one participant.
numbers: P7 used IDE AI heavily; AI-generated fix attempt failed and P7 fixed manually; S1's Claude Sonnet query fixed a syntax error faster than docs.
quote: since it is AI-generated, we do not actually know how to handle
limits: Only a few participants used LLMs; this is not an LLM-vs-human test.
agent_relevance: Humans use LLMs for fact lookup, not for building the model. Our agent must build its own model from real output.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: A Text-Based Environment for Interactive Debugging
finding: Giving an LLM agent the pdb debugger from step 1 helps on repo-scale bugs only for strong models. Weak models get worse.
numbers: SWE-bench-Lite (300 tasks), mean of 3 runs. Claude 3.7 Sonnet: rewrite-only 37.2%, debug (pdb from start) 48.4%, debug(5) (pdb after 5th rewrite) 52.1%. Llama-3.3-70B: 2.4 / 4.0 / 4.8. GPT-4o-mini: 4.0 / 3.5 / 6.2.
quote: accessing the pdb tool at the beginning could to some extent harm the overall performance
limits: Table columns were garbled in text extraction; Claude and Llama rows read cleanly, others less sure. Authors say prompts were minimal and untuned.
agent_relevance: Unlock runtime-inspection tools after the plain loop stalls (post-impasse), not at the start. Fits G1.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: A Text-Based Environment for Interactive Debugging
finding: On easy code-generation tasks, debugger access made no clear difference.
numbers: Aider benchmark, 3 runs. GPT-4o: rewrite 69.7 vs debug 72.9. o3-mini: 95.2 vs 94.2. Llama-3.3-70B: 58.4 vs 56.9 vs 61.4 (debug(5)). Llama-3.2-3B about 4% in all arms.
limits: Aider logic is simple; authors suggest agents lacked a strategy for pdb use.
agent_relevance: Evidence gathering has a cost; do not run it when the output already explains the bug.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: A Text-Based Environment for Interactive Debugging
finding: Weaker models rewrite the same code chunk again and again. Stronger models read the error and form the right model of the cause at once. A Claude 3.7 trace looks like a human debugging session.
numbers: Mini-nightmare (10 hand-made bugs), patcher task: GPT-4o and Llama-3.3-70B got zero successes; R1-Distill-Llama-70B and Claude 3.7 saw it was a line-number range bug. Claude trace: view, set breakpoint, print 5 variables, clear breakpoint, one rewrite.
limits: Ten tasks only; qualitative reading of a few traces.
agent_relevance: Failure mode to detect in code: repeated edits to the same lines without new evidence. That should force a return to S2.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: A Text-Based Environment for Interactive Debugging
finding: A model can use the debugger to test a belief about the system and correct it. Claude 3.7 found a Python 2 vs 3 rounding difference this way.
numbers: shopping_cart task: GPT-4o and Llama-3.3-70B patched the discount logic but failed the test (round of 10.225 differs: Py2 away-from-zero, Py3 ties-to-even); Claude 3.7 used pdb to test the hypothesis and switched to round-half-up.
limits: Single task, single trace.
agent_relevance: A belief about environment semantics (version) can be wrong while the model of program logic is right. Verify by running.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: A Text-Based Environment for Interactive Debugging
finding: Reasoning models overthink in interactive loops. They repeat reasoning chunks even after a reasonable answer.
numbers: R1-distill models produced far more response tokens per episode on Aider (Figure 5, no exact count extracted); R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 82.7% rewrite vs GPT-4o 69.7%.
limits: Qualitative claim by authors.
agent_relevance: Per-step token caps matter when evidence gathering is sequential.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: A Text-Based Environment for Interactive Debugging
finding: Authors name two reasons agents use debug tools poorly: minimal agent design and scarcity of human debugging traces in training data.
numbers: No ablation; stated as belief.
limits: Not tested directly.
agent_relevance: A scaffold can supply the missing procedure (when to inspect, what to log) without training.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: Interface design for gathering evidence changes results a lot with a fixed model. A small set of view/search/edit commands beats plain shell.
numbers: GPT-4 Turbo: 12.47% of 2,294 SWE-bench tasks (previous best non-interactive 3.8%); on SWE-bench Lite ablation, 10.7 points above shell-only baseline; Claude 3 Opus 10.5% on full set.
limits: Ablation on 300 Lite tasks with large error bars (+-3.0 to +-7.7).
agent_relevance: Evidence-gathering tools are part of the scaffold; design them for compact, specific feedback.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: Search presentation matters. Summarised search (list of files) beat step-through search; showing too much or too little file text hurt.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, GPT-4 Turbo: summarized search 18.0, iterative 12.0 (-6.0), no search 15.7 (-2.3); viewer 100 lines 18.0, 30 lines 14.3, full file 12.7; last-5 observations 18.0, full history 15.0.
limits: Single model for ablation; wide error bars.
agent_relevance: Keep the working view of code compact (about 100 lines) and history short; this supports a small running model in S2.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: A lint check on each edit stops cascading errors.
numbers: Edit with linting 18.0; edit without linting 15.0 (-3.0); no edit command 10.3 (-7.7).
limits: Same caveats.
agent_relevance: Code-checked guardrails after each action (G2) pay off.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: A fixed pipeline without an agent loop (localise, repair, validate) matched agents on SWE-bench Lite at lower cost.
numbers: GPT-4o: 32.00% (96 of 300) at $0.70 average cost; highest among open-source approaches at the time.
limits: Fixed hierarchical localisation; no free exploration.
agent_relevance: The model of the system can be built by staged narrowing (files, then classes, then lines) controlled by code.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: Hierarchical localisation: the combined method is best. A skeleton view of code beat full files for related-element search.
numbers: File level contains-GT: prompting 78.67%, embedding 67.67% (70.33% rising to 81.67% with irrelevant-file filtering). Related elements: complete file 53.67%, skeleton 58.33% with fewer lines (698 vs 778).
limits: Metric is whether the true location stays in the candidate set, not final fix rate.
agent_relevance: Show the agent structure (skeletons) before bodies. This cuts context while keeping the true site in view.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) AutoCodeRover: Autonomous Program Improvement
finding: Code search over program structure (classes, methods), plus spectrum-based fault localisation from tests, improves issue resolution.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: AutoCodeRover 19% (57/300); with SBFL (ACR-sbfl) 22.00% (66); SWE-agent 18% in same comparison; full SWE-bench: 12.42% @1, 17.96% @3.
limits: SBFL needs failing and passing tests; GPT-4 backbone.
agent_relevance: Test-coverage evidence is a cheap second source for the system model besides reading.

source: Jimenez et al. (2024) SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
finding: Finding the right code is a main bottleneck. With BM25 retrieval of files, the best model resolved very few issues.
numbers: Claude 2 with BM25 retrieval resolved 1.96% of issues. BM25 retrieved a superset of oracle files in about 40% of instances at 27k tokens and none of the oracle files in almost half.
limits: Non-agentic retrieval baseline from 2023; later agents are far higher.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of the right context is where the system model starts; wrong context makes the model wrong from step one.

source: Jimenez et al. (2024) SWE-bench
finding: Longer input hurts: models do worse as total context length grows.
numbers: Section on context length: Claude 2 performance falls as context grows (Figure 5; exact values not extracted).
limits: Chat models; one family.
agent_relevance: Prefer small targeted context over dumping files.

source: Liu et al. (2024) CodeMind: A Framework to Challenge LLMs for Code Reasoning
finding: Models can simulate some code execution but do worse with nesting, non-primitive types and class dependencies. Bug-repair success was not correlated with the code-reasoning tasks for most models.
numbers: 13 LLMs, 4 benchmarks; tasks: execution, specification and dynamic semantics reasoning. Except for advanced frontier models, others did not use code reasoning in bug repair (authors' claim).
limits: Reasoning measured on given inputs; repair measured separately.
agent_relevance: The model's internal running of code is unreliable; run the code and read real output (G2).

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval
finding: Predicting the output or input of short Python functions is hard even for the best models in early 2024.
numbers: GPT-4 pass@1 67% on CRUXEval-I (input) and 63% on CRUXEval-O (output); best open-source 47% and 44%.
limits: Short functions; no repo context; early-2024 models.
agent_relevance: Mental simulation of small code is a weak point; do not trust the agent's unrun predictions of behaviour.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Repair is bottlenecked by the quality of the model's explanation of why the code fails. Stronger feedback or a human explanation lifts results.
numbers: Repair success with GPT-4 feedback 33.30% overall vs human feedback 52.60% (intro 42.64 vs 62.21; interview 19.33 vs 45.67; competition 3.67 vs 14.67). GPT-4 on APPS: 10 samples then 1 repair each = 1.05x pass@20; 2 samples then 10 repairs = 0.97x pass@22.
limits: Single-function tasks (HumanEval, APPS); small human study.
agent_relevance: Where the model's diagnosis is poor, a code-produced diagnosis (traces, expected vs actual diffs) is worth more than more repair attempts.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without an external signal, asking a model to review its own answer usually does not help and can hurt. Earlier gains came from oracle labels or weak first prompts.
numbers: Paper reports performance after intrinsic self-correction mostly fails to improve and sometimes drops; gains in prior work vanish without oracle labels (per-benchmark numbers not extracted).
limits: Reasoning tasks (math, QA), not code with test feedback.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: revise only from real output, not from self-critique.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) LDB: Debug like a Human
finding: Giving the model runtime values of variables after each basic block, and asking it to verify each block against the task, improves debugging.
numbers: Up to 9.8% gain across HumanEval, MBPP and TransCoder; block-level beat line-level and whole-function; TransCoder hard-level problems gain 9.1%.
limits: Programs from earlier LLMs (GPT-3.5 etc.), small functions.
agent_relevance: A direct version of building a model from execution traces: block-level state checks are the right grain.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Rubber-duck style: the model explains its code in words and reads execution results, then fixes. Works with few-shot examples.
numbers: Spider: +2-3% with explanation, +9% on hardest level; TransCoder and MBPP: up to +12% with unit tests; GPT-4 without unit tests on MBPP +3.6%, others about 1%.
limits: Gain with no test feedback is small; most value comes from execution feedback.
agent_relevance: Explaining code line by line is a cheap way to refresh S2; most value arrives with real execution feedback.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Agent stores verbal reflections on failures in memory and uses them in the next try; a running memory of what went wrong.
numbers: 91% pass@1 on HumanEval (abstract); gains over baselines of 22% in AlfWorld, 20% in HotPotQA, 11% on HumanEval.
limits: Relies on test results as success signal; Olausson and Huang show self-feedback alone is weak.
agent_relevance: A scaffold-level analogue to updating the mental model after a failed fix, anchored on the failing test.
